curriculum: NaCCA Religious and Moral Education Curriculum for Primary Schools, September 2019
accessibility_note: Teachers may read prompts aloud. Accept oral, written, drawn or role-play responses where suitable. Assess curriculum knowledge, not personal belief. Use teacher-provided accounts; no hazardous activities, worship-site visits or private religious disclosure are required.
curriculum_note: Printed indicator codes are preserved where clear. Some codes and statements in the curriculum PDF have spacing or punctuation inconsistencies; see indicator notes.

indicators.statement: Explain the nature of God as the Creator.

questions.prompt: According to the class lesson, who is described as the originator of all things?
questions.answer: God
questions.hint: Recall the description of God as Creator in the class account.
questions.explanation: The curriculum presents God as the originator of all things.
questions.misconception_note: Assess knowledge of the teaching, not personal belief.

questions.prompt: Name two examples of things the class account describes as created by God.
answer: Any two appropriate examples, such as human beings, trees, animals or water bodies.
questions.hint: Think of living things and features of the natural world.
questions.explanation: Learners recall examples in the curriculum exemplar.
questions.misconception_note: Accept examples consistent with the lesson.

questions.prompt: Which is a natural feature named as an example in the curriculum?
questions.answer: A water body
questions.hint: Choose a feature of nature.
questions.explanation: Water bodies are among the examples listed in the curriculum.
questions.misconception_note: Distinguish natural things from human-made objects.

questions.prompt: Learners observe trees, animals and a stream in a safe school area. What are they doing for this lesson?
options: Observing examples of the natural world
questions.answer: Observing examples of the natural world
questions.hint: Think of the curriculum's nature-observation activity.
questions.explanation: Observation helps learners identify examples for classroom discussion.
questions.misconception_note: A school-based observation is enough; no special site visit is required.

questions.prompt: What does the word “Creator” mean in this lesson?
answer: The originator or maker of creation, as described in the religious account studied.
questions.hint: Use the wording from the lesson.
questions.explanation: The curriculum describes God as the originator of all things.
questions.misconception_note: Accept a clear paraphrase.

questions.prompt: Match each example to a category: (1) tree; (2) animal; (3) lake. Categories: A. water body; B. plant; C. animal.
questions.hint: Sort each item by what it is.
questions.explanation: The items are examples of the natural world.
questions.misconception_note: This checks classification, not personal belief.

questions.prompt: Why might a class observe natural things before discussing creation?
options: Observation gives concrete examples for discussion
It proves every learner has the same belief
questions.answer: Observation gives concrete examples for discussion
questions.hint: Think about how seeing examples can support learning.
questions.explanation: Observation can help learners document examples of the natural world.
questions.misconception_note: Do not claim that observation proves a religious belief.

questions.prompt: Describe one example of creation mentioned in your class lesson.
answer: A clear example consistent with the teacher-provided lesson.
questions.hint: Name one natural thing or living thing studied.
questions.explanation: Learners practise describing the examples discussed.
questions.misconception_note: Oral answers are acceptable.

questions.prompt: A learner writes down a tree and a bird after an observation. What should the learner do next in the activity?
options: Share the findings for class discussion
Claim the observation settles all religious questions
questions.answer: Share the findings for class discussion
questions.hint: Recall the group reporting step.
questions.explanation: The exemplar asks learners to put findings together and present them.
questions.misconception_note: Observe without disturbing living things.

questions.prompt: Draw one natural example discussed in class and label it.
answer: A recognisable drawing or alternative oral description of a class example, with a suitable label.
questions.hint: Choose an example such as a tree, animal or water body.
questions.explanation: A labelled drawing communicates an observation.
questions.misconception_note: Assess the example and label, not artistic skill.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches the curriculum's description of God as Creator?
options: God is described as the originator of all things
A tree is described as the originator of all things
The lesson says nature should be damaged
questions.answer: God is described as the originator of all things
questions.hint: Recall the content standard wording.
questions.explanation: The curriculum frames the lesson around God as Creator.
questions.misconception_note: Phrase responses as curriculum knowledge rather than a required personal profession.

questions.prompt: Give one reason a group might combine its observations before presenting them.
answer: To organise the examples and share a fuller set of findings with the class.
questions.hint: Think about what group discussion adds.
questions.explanation: Combining findings supports communication and class discussion.
questions.misconception_note: Accept other reasonable explanations.

questions.prompt: Match the classroom activity to its purpose: (1) observing; (2) recording; (3) presenting. Purposes: A. sharing findings; B. noticing examples; C. keeping a note of what was seen.
questions.hint: Put the steps with their purposes.
questions.explanation: Observation, recording and presentation form a simple learning process.
questions.misconception_note: Accept equivalent descriptions.

questions.prompt: A learner sees a small animal during observation. Which action is safest and most respectful?
options: Observe it without touching or disturbing it
Take it away from its habitat
questions.answer: Observe it without touching or disturbing it
questions.hint: Keep learners and wildlife safe.
questions.explanation: Observation does not require handling or harming living things.
questions.misconception_note: Never require contact with wildlife.

questions.prompt: Explain how observing natural things can help a learner describe examples from the lesson.
answer: Observation lets learners notice and name examples they can discuss or record.
questions.hint: Connect looking carefully with naming examples.
questions.explanation: Observation supports accurate description and reporting.
questions.misconception_note: Do not frame this as proof of anyone's personal faith.

questions.prompt: Which is a useful way to report group observations?
options: List the examples clearly and explain them
Add objects that were not observed
questions.answer: List the examples clearly and explain them
questions.hint: Choose a clear and honest report.
questions.explanation: The curriculum encourages groups to present findings for discussion.
questions.misconception_note: Encourage evidence-based reporting.

questions.prompt: Name one thing a learner could record during a safe observation of the school environment.
answer: A natural example such as a plant, animal or water feature, described accurately.
questions.hint: Record something actually seen or otherwise supplied by the teacher.
questions.explanation: Recording supports the class discussion of examples.
questions.misconception_note: Do not require a field trip; a picture or teacher-provided observation can be used.

questions.prompt: In a group, role-play presenting an observation of one natural example to classmates. One learner is the reporter and another asks a respectful question.
answer: The reporter names and describes an appropriate example; the listener asks a relevant question politely.
questions.hint: Use a classroom or imagined safe observation.
questions.explanation: The activity practises clear reporting and discussion.
questions.misconception_note: No worship, travel or handling of objects is required.

questions.prompt: Give an oral, written or drawn response explaining the class description of God as Creator and name two examples used in the lesson.
answer: A response describing God as originator of all things in the class account, with two suitable examples.
questions.hint: Use the wording and examples studied.
questions.explanation: This assesses recall and explanation of the indicator.
questions.misconception_note: Assess understanding of the curriculum rather than personal belief.

questions.prompt: Which response best follows the lesson's observation activity?
options: Record examples carefully and discuss them with the group
Invent observations to impress the class
Damage natural things to study them
Require classmates to state a personal belief
questions.answer: Record examples carefully and discuss them with the group
questions.hint: Choose safe, accurate, collaborative learning.
questions.explanation: The exemplar asks learners to document, combine and present observations.
questions.misconception_note: Keep activities safe and inclusive.

indicators.statement: Identify the uniqueness of humankind from other creatures.
indicators.code_note: The PDF prints this indicator as B4.1.1.2.1 within the section; retain its printed form despite punctuation/spacing irregularities.

questions.prompt: Which ability is named in the curriculum as a characteristic of humankind?
questions.answer: Thinking
questions.hint: Choose a characteristic connected to reasoning.
questions.explanation: The curriculum lists thinking ability among human characteristics.
questions.misconception_note: The task is to identify listed distinctions, not to claim humans are the only beings with any form of cognition.

questions.prompt: Name one characteristic of humankind listed in the class material.
answer: Thinking ability, ability to speak, or knowing what is good and evil.
questions.hint: Recall the curriculum's examples.
questions.explanation: These are the characteristics named in the exemplar.
questions.misconception_note: Accept any one accurate example.

questions.prompt: Which feature does the curriculum specifically mention as a human characteristic?
questions.answer: Ability to speak
questions.hint: Choose a communication ability in the example list.
questions.explanation: The exemplar names the ability to speak.
questions.misconception_note: Avoid suggesting that all people communicate in the same way; signed and augmentative communication are valid.

questions.prompt: A group is comparing a human being, an animal and a plant. Which method best fits the lesson?
options: List characteristics of each and discuss similarities and differences respectfully
Say one living thing has no value
Harm an animal to compare it
questions.answer: List characteristics of each and discuss similarities and differences respectfully
questions.hint: Use observation and careful comparison.
questions.explanation: The curriculum asks learners to compare humans with animals and plants.
questions.misconception_note: Do not harm or demean living things.

questions.prompt: Name one way people can communicate besides speaking aloud.
answer: Writing, signing, gestures, pictures, communication devices or another valid method.
questions.hint: Think of different ways people share ideas.
questions.explanation: People communicate in varied ways; the lesson should be inclusive.
questions.misconception_note: Do not treat speech as a measure of a person's worth or ability.

questions.prompt: Match each example to the broad category: (1) human thinking; (2) plant roots; (3) animal movement. Categories: A. example of a plant feature; B. example of an animal action; C. characteristic listed for humankind.
questions.hint: Identify whether each example refers to a human, plant or animal feature.
questions.explanation: Classification helps learners compare living things.
questions.misconception_note: Real organisms have many traits; these are simple classroom examples.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to compare humans with other creatures?
options: Decide that one kind of life has no value
questions.answer: Notice similarities and differences
questions.hint: A comparison looks at what is alike and what is different.
questions.explanation: Comparison is the learning activity described in the curriculum.
questions.misconception_note: Comparison should not be used to justify disrespect or harm.

questions.prompt: State one characteristic listed for humankind and explain it in simple words.
answer: One listed characteristic with a reasonable explanation.
questions.hint: Choose thinking, communication, or knowing right from wrong.
questions.explanation: Learners identify and explain a human characteristic from the lesson.
questions.misconception_note: Allow accessible oral, signed or communication-device responses.

questions.prompt: A learner says a classmate who communicates without speech is not fully human. What is the correct response?
options: That is false; people communicate in different ways and have equal dignity
Agree because speech is required to be human
Exclude the classmate from the lesson
questions.answer: That is false; people communicate in different ways and have equal dignity
questions.hint: The curriculum example must not be used to exclude people.
questions.explanation: A listed characteristic is not a test of anyone's humanity or worth.
questions.misconception_note: Reject ableist interpretations; all learners are included.

questions.prompt: Draw a human and another living thing, then label one difference and one similarity discussed in class.
answer: A respectful comparison with one plausible similarity and one appropriate difference, communicated by labels or orally.
questions.hint: For example, both can be living, while they may differ in how they communicate or grow.
questions.explanation: The curriculum suggests drawing and comparing a human and an animal.
questions.misconception_note: Assess comparison, not artistic detail; avoid ranking worth.

questions.prompt: Which idea is an example of knowing what is good and evil, as named in the lesson?
options: Thinking about whether an action is right or harmful
questions.answer: Thinking about whether an action is right or harmful
questions.hint: Choose a moral judgement.
questions.explanation: The curriculum lists knowing what is good and evil among human characteristics.
questions.misconception_note: Discuss this as a lesson example, not as a claim that every person always makes the same judgement.

questions.prompt: Give one similarity between humans and another living thing.
answer: A reasonable similarity, such as both being living things or needing resources to live.
questions.hint: Look for a feature both share.
questions.explanation: Comparisons include similarities as well as differences.
questions.misconception_note: Accept scientifically reasonable examples.

questions.prompt: Match each way of communicating to an example: (1) sign language; (2) writing; (3) speech. Examples: A. spoken words; B. written words; C. hand signs and movements.
questions.hint: Match each communication method with how it works.
questions.explanation: People communicate in different ways.
questions.misconception_note: Treat all communication methods as valid.

questions.prompt: A group notices that plants grow and humans grow too. What has the group found?
options: Proof that plants and humans are identical
questions.answer: A similarity between living things
questions.hint: Both examples share a feature.
questions.explanation: Growth is a reasonable similarity for classroom comparison.
questions.misconception_note: A similarity does not mean two kinds of living things are identical.

questions.prompt: In pairs, role-play a respectful group discussion comparing one human characteristic with one plant or animal feature. Include one similarity and one difference.
answer: Learners communicate one relevant similarity and one relevant difference respectfully.
questions.hint: Use examples from class and let each partner speak or communicate in their preferred mode.
questions.explanation: The activity practises comparison and collaborative communication.
questions.misconception_note: Do not rank the value of living things or exclude non-speaking learners.

rubric.comparison: 0–2: gives a plausible similarity and difference

questions.prompt: Which is the fairest conclusion after comparing people and other living things?
options: Different characteristics can be described without saying any life has no value
Differences prove one group should be harmed
Only one way of communicating counts
questions.answer: Different characteristics can be described without saying any life has no value
questions.hint: Choose a respectful conclusion based on comparison.
questions.explanation: The lesson asks learners to identify characteristics, not justify harm or exclusion.
questions.misconception_note: Emphasise dignity and care.

questions.prompt: Why should a group use evidence when comparing humans and other creatures?
answer: Evidence makes the comparison accurate and helps avoid unsupported claims.
questions.hint: Think about what makes a comparison fair.
questions.explanation: Careful observations support reliable comparisons.
questions.misconception_note: Accept concise answers.

questions.prompt: Explain one reason people should treat other living things responsibly while studying them.
answer: A reasonable response such as protecting living things, avoiding harm, or respecting creation as taught in class.
questions.hint: Consider care and responsibility.
questions.explanation: The curriculum's values include care and responsible stewardship.
questions.misconception_note: No personal religious affirmation is required.

questions.prompt: Present a comparison of humans with an animal or plant, using words, a chart or a labelled drawing. Include two characteristics and one similarity or difference.
answer: A clear comparison using relevant characteristics and at least one sensible similarity or difference.
questions.hint: Use examples from the curriculum and class discussion.
questions.explanation: This assesses the ability to identify human uniqueness through comparison.
questions.misconception_note: Do not infer a learner's worth or ability from the comparison.

questions.prompt: Which response best reflects the indicator about humankind's uniqueness?
options: Identify and compare characteristics such as thinking, communication and moral understanding
Claim that people who communicate differently are less human
Say animals and plants should be harmed
questions.answer: Identify and compare characteristics such as thinking, communication and moral understanding
questions.hint: Choose the option based on the class examples and respectful comparison.
questions.explanation: The indicator asks learners to identify human characteristics in comparison with other creatures.
questions.misconception_note: Teach the examples inclusively and do not make them tests of human dignity.

indicators.statement: Discuss the effects of human activities on the environment.
indicators.code_note: The PDF displays this indicator with irregular spacing and punctuation; code normalised to the evident annotation sequence B4.1.2.1.1.

questions.prompt: Which activity is listed as harmful to the environment in the curriculum?
questions.answer: Illegal mining
questions.hint: Choose an activity the curriculum names as destructive.
questions.explanation: Illegal mining is given as an example of an activity that can damage the environment.
questions.misconception_note: Keep examples age-appropriate and focused on environmental effects.

questions.prompt: Name one human activity that can harm the environment, as discussed in class.
answer: Illegal mining, deforestation, water pollution or air pollution.
questions.hint: Recall the examples from the lesson.
questions.explanation: The curriculum names these as harmful human activities.
questions.misconception_note: Accept other accurate examples discussed by the teacher.

questions.prompt: What is deforestation?
questions.answer: Indiscriminate cutting down of trees
questions.hint: The word refers to loss of forests or trees.
questions.explanation: The curriculum names indiscriminate cutting down of trees as deforestation.
questions.misconception_note: Accept a clear age-appropriate definition.

questions.prompt: A community stream becomes polluted by waste. Which effect could follow?
options: Water quality may be harmed and people or animals may be affected
questions.answer: Water quality may be harmed and people or animals may be affected
questions.hint: Think about what clean water is needed for.
questions.explanation: Pollution of water bodies can harm the environment and living things.
questions.misconception_note: Use careful wording; effects depend on the pollutant and situation.

questions.prompt: Give one effect of harmful human activities on the environment mentioned in the curriculum.
answer: Heat, floods, rainstorms, less rainfall, famine or drought.
questions.hint: Recall the listed effects connected to climate and weather.
questions.explanation: These are effects named in the curriculum exemplar.
questions.misconception_note: Accept other accurate impacts taught in class.

questions.prompt: Match the activity with the environmental concern: (1) cutting many trees; (2) releasing harmful substances into a river; (3) releasing smoke into the air. Concerns: A. water pollution; B. air pollution; C. deforestation.
questions.hint: Match each action with the affected part of the environment.
questions.explanation: Different activities can affect forests, water and air.
questions.misconception_note: Do not imply these are the only causes of environmental harm.

questions.prompt: Which outcome is listed in the curriculum as a possible effect of environmental damage?
options: More clean water in every place
questions.answer: Drought
questions.hint: Choose a listed climate or weather-related effect.
questions.explanation: Drought is named among the possible effects.
questions.misconception_note: Avoid implying a single activity directly causes every listed outcome in every place.

questions.prompt: Explain one way cutting down many trees can affect the environment.
answer: A reasonable effect such as loss of tree cover or habitat, increased erosion, or effects on rainfall, where covered in class.
questions.hint: Think about what trees provide to soil, animals and people.
questions.explanation: Learners discuss effects of human activities on the environment.
questions.misconception_note: Accept scientifically sound explanations and careful phrasing.

questions.prompt: Learners see smoke from several sources near a settlement. Which environmental issue should they discuss?
questions.answer: Air pollution
questions.hint: Identify which part of the environment smoke affects.
questions.explanation: Air pollution is one of the curriculum's examples.
questions.misconception_note: Do not ask learners to approach smoke or hazardous areas.

questions.prompt: Draw a simple cause-and-effect picture showing one harmful human activity and one possible environmental effect. Label both.
answer: A reasonable activity-effect pair with labels, such as tree cutting and loss of tree cover, or pollution and harmed water quality.
questions.hint: Use one cause and one effect from class.
questions.explanation: A labelled diagram helps show a relationship between an activity and an effect.
questions.misconception_note: Avoid asserting a causal link that the lesson has not supported.

questions.prompt: Why should learners discuss both human activities and their effects?
options: To understand how actions can affect the environment
questions.answer: To understand how actions can affect the environment
questions.hint: Think of the purpose of examining cause and effect.
questions.explanation: The indicator focuses on discussing effects of human activities.
questions.misconception_note: Keep the discussion evidence-based rather than blaming individuals without context.

questions.prompt: Name one way learners can study environmental effects without going near a dangerous site.
answer: Use teacher-provided pictures, videos, charts, readings or safe classroom data.
questions.hint: Choose a classroom resource.
questions.explanation: The curriculum allows pictures and video clips as learning resources.
questions.misconception_note: Never require a visit to an unsafe mining, pollution or disaster site.

questions.prompt: Match the environmental effect to a suitable description: (1) flood; (2) drought; (3) air pollution. Descriptions: A. harmful substances in the air; B. too little water or rainfall over a period; C. water covering land that is usually dry.
questions.hint: Match each term to its simple meaning.
questions.explanation: Understanding the terms helps learners discuss environmental effects.
questions.misconception_note: Accept simple descriptions; avoid technical detail beyond the lesson.

questions.prompt: A class is asked to explain whether an activity affected a local environment, but they have no evidence. What is the best next step?
options: Use reliable information or observations before drawing a conclusion
questions.answer: Use reliable information or observations before drawing a conclusion
questions.hint: Good discussion depends on facts.
questions.explanation: The curriculum encourages learners to discuss environmental effects using information.
questions.misconception_note: Distinguish evidence from assumption.

questions.prompt: Role-play a short classroom discussion in which one learner names a harmful activity, another describes a possible effect, and a third asks how the claim could be checked safely.
answer: Learners identify an activity, state a plausible effect and propose a safe evidence source.
questions.hint: Use a class example and resources such as a chart or teacher-provided report.
questions.explanation: This practises discussion, cause-and-effect reasoning and safe inquiry.
questions.misconception_note: Do not act out hazardous activity or visit dangerous locations.

questions.prompt: Which response uses careful language about environmental effects?
options: Some harmful activities can contribute to environmental problems
One activity always causes every flood everywhere
Environmental damage cannot affect living things
questions.answer: Some harmful activities can contribute to environmental problems
questions.hint: Choose the statement that avoids overclaiming.
questions.explanation: Environmental outcomes can have multiple causes, so explanations should be careful.
questions.misconception_note: Use accurate, appropriately qualified claims.

questions.prompt: Why can pollution of water bodies be harmful?
answer: It can make water unsafe or damage habitats and living things, depending on the pollution.
questions.hint: Think about who and what depend on water.
questions.explanation: Pollution may harm people, animals, plants or habitats.
questions.misconception_note: Accept a reasonable explanation without requiring technical vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Describe one possible connection between environmental damage and people's lives, using a class example.
answer: A relevant connection, such as pollution affecting water use or drought reducing water availability or crops.
questions.hint: Connect one environmental effect to a need people have.
questions.explanation: The curriculum links environmental effects to issues such as famine and drought.
questions.misconception_note: Allow careful paraphrase and evidence-based examples.

questions.prompt: Present a short cause-and-effect explanation of one human activity and its possible environmental effect, using an oral explanation, paragraph or labelled diagram.
answer: A relevant harmful activity paired with a plausible, accurately explained environmental effect.
questions.hint: Use a class example and explain the connection simply.
questions.explanation: This directly assesses discussion of effects of human activities.
questions.misconception_note: Do not require fieldwork or exposure to hazardous materials.

rubric.effect: 0–2: identifies and explains a plausible effect

questions.prompt: Which response best summarises the indicator?
options: Discuss how human activities such as deforestation or pollution can affect the environment
Carry out illegal mining to observe it
questions.answer: Discuss how human activities such as deforestation or pollution can affect the environment
questions.hint: Choose the option focused on the curriculum outcome.
questions.explanation: Learners discuss harmful activities and their possible effects.
questions.misconception_note: Use safe resources and evidence-based discussion.

indicators.statement: Name the various forms of worship.

questions.prompt: Which religious groups are named in the curriculum for this unit?
options: Christianity, Islam and African Traditional Religion
questions.answer: Christianity, Islam and African Traditional Religion
questions.hint: Recall the three major religious groups studied in Ghana.
questions.explanation: The curriculum refers to the three major religious groups in Ghana.
questions.misconception_note: Use respectful, accurate names for each tradition.

questions.prompt: Name one form or activity of worship studied in class.
answer: A form or activity accurately discussed in the class lesson, such as prayer, singing, recitation or communal worship.
questions.hint: Use an example from a tradition taught by the teacher.
questions.explanation: Learners identify forms of worship from the traditions studied.
questions.misconception_note: No learner needs to perform worship or disclose personal practice.

questions.prompt: What can pictures of worship help learners do in this lesson?
options: Observe and discuss different forms of worship
Decide that all worship looks exactly the same
questions.answer: Observe and discuss different forms of worship
questions.hint: Think of pictures as learning resources.
questions.explanation: The exemplar uses pictures to support observation and discussion.
questions.misconception_note: Pictures support learning; they are not a basis for judging believers.

questions.prompt: A learner is unsure about a worship practice shown in a class picture. What should the learner do?
options: Ask a respectful question and listen to the explanation
questions.answer: Ask a respectful question and listen to the explanation
questions.hint: Choose a respectful way to learn.
questions.explanation: Questions and discussion help learners understand practices fairly.
questions.misconception_note: Do not require reenactment of sacred practices.

questions.prompt: Why should forms of worship be described respectfully?
answer: To represent traditions fairly and support respectful learning among classmates.
questions.hint: Think about how learners from different backgrounds should be treated.
questions.explanation: Respect supports inclusive learning about diverse religious practices.
questions.misconception_note: Respect does not require agreement or personal participation.

questions.prompt: Match the classroom source to how learners use it: (1) picture; (2) teacher explanation; (3) group notes. Uses: A. record ideas; B. observe a scene; C. clarify context.
questions.hint: Match each resource to its purpose.
questions.explanation: Different resources help learners study worship practices.
questions.misconception_note: Accept equivalent descriptions.

questions.prompt: Which is an appropriate way to learn about a form of worship without taking part in it?
options: Study a teacher-provided description or picture
Force a classmate to demonstrate it
Copy a sacred act as a joke
Assume all traditions practise it identically
questions.answer: Study a teacher-provided description or picture
questions.hint: Choose observation rather than compelled participation.
questions.explanation: The curriculum suggests using pictures and discussion.
questions.misconception_note: RME assessment should not require personal worship.

questions.prompt: Describe one worship activity shown or explained in a class resource.
answer: A neutral, accurate description of an activity in the resource.
questions.hint: Say what people are doing, without judging them.
questions.explanation: Learners practise naming and describing forms of worship.
questions.misconception_note: Accept oral, signed or supported communication.

questions.prompt: A group is making notes about a worship picture. Which note is most suitable?
options: A neutral description of the activity visible in the picture
A guess presented as a fact
A claim that one group is superior
questions.answer: A neutral description of the activity visible in the picture
questions.hint: Record what can be observed accurately.
questions.explanation: Observation should be descriptive and respectful.
questions.misconception_note: Separate what is seen from what is inferred.

questions.prompt: Draw a neutral classroom diagram showing how learners can study a worship practice using a picture, notes and discussion. Do not depict sacred acts if unsure.
answer: A simple diagram showing observation, note-taking and discussion, or a respectful labelled alternative.
questions.hint: You may draw learners looking at a picture and talking together.
questions.explanation: The task focuses on learning methods rather than reproducing worship.
questions.misconception_note: Do not assess sacred imagery or artistic skill.

questions.prompt: Which statement is accurate about worship in the three major religions studied?
options: Forms of worship may differ among traditions
Every group worships in exactly the same way
Only one tradition may be discussed
questions.answer: Forms of worship may differ among traditions
questions.hint: Think about diversity in religious practice.
questions.explanation: The curriculum asks learners to study forms in several religious groups.
questions.misconception_note: Avoid stereotypes; describe the practices actually taught.

questions.prompt: Name one respectful question a learner could ask about a worship practice.
answer: A curious, non-mocking question about what the practice means or when it takes place.
questions.hint: Ask to understand, not to challenge or ridicule.
questions.explanation: Respectful questions support learning about practices.
questions.misconception_note: Accept varied questions that do not demand private disclosure.

questions.prompt: Match the learning action to the skill: (1) look carefully at a picture; (2) write down what is seen; (3) explain a practice to a partner. Skills: A. communicate; B. observe; C. record.
questions.hint: Identify whether the learner is observing, recording or communicating.
questions.explanation: These skills support study of worship forms.
questions.misconception_note: Accept equivalent terms.

questions.prompt: A classmate declines to act out a religious practice during role-play. What is a respectful response?
options: Offer an alternative such as describing a picture or reading a neutral account
questions.answer: Offer an alternative such as describing a picture or reading a neutral account
questions.hint: Learning can be shown without personal religious performance.
questions.explanation: Accessible alternatives allow learners to meet the learning goal respectfully.
questions.misconception_note: Never compel worship or sacred reenactment.

questions.prompt: Role-play a respectful classroom conversation: one learner describes a teacher-provided picture of worship, and another asks a neutral question.
answer: Learners describe visible details accurately and ask or answer a respectful question.
questions.hint: Use a neutral picture or fictional classroom resource.
questions.explanation: The activity practises description and respectful discussion.
questions.misconception_note: Do not imitate sacred acts or require learners to identify their religion.

questions.prompt: What should a learner avoid when describing another group's worship?
questions.answer: Unsupported assumptions and insulting language
questions.hint: Choose what undermines fair description.
questions.explanation: Descriptions should be accurate and respectful.
questions.misconception_note: Avoid treating a single example as universal for a whole religion.

questions.prompt: How can a teacher help learners understand a worship activity if a picture is unclear?
answer: Provide context, explain the activity or use another reliable classroom resource.
questions.hint: Use a reliable source rather than guessing.
questions.explanation: Context improves accurate understanding.
questions.misconception_note: Accept any reasonable source-based approach.

questions.prompt: Explain one difference a class might observe between two forms of worship, based only on the resources studied.
answer: A specific, neutral difference supported by the class material.
questions.hint: Compare an observable feature, not the worth of the traditions.
